extracted.intended_audience: students, educated lay readers, and citizens interested in scientific method and public policy
extracted.subtask_description: A chapter-length exposition of what the scientific method is, its proper domain, its limits (and the proper confession of ignorance), the disciplined role of imagination in discovery, and the consequences of scientific method for social and moral judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific method (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: The orderly classification of facts followed by the recognition of their relationship and recurring sequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is presented as the core method: classify facts accurately, then deduce relationships and recurring sequences. The discovery of law follows from this process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: The scientific judgment is the judgment based upon this recognition and free from personal bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scientific judgment, grounded in classification and recognition of relationships, aims at impartiality and tends to produce practical unanimity when different individuals approach the same facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope / domain of science
rubrics_metrics.description: Wherever there is the slightest possibility for the human mind to know, there is a legitimate problem of science; the whole range of phenomena, mental as well as physical, is its field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Science claims the universe as its field and rejects artificial limits (illustrated by Galileo's history). The word 'science' is used broadly for all reasoning about facts proceeding from classification to law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confession of ignorance and patience
rubrics_metrics.description: Science frankly admits its ignorance in many fields and requires long and patient toil for classification before drawing conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where classification is insufficient or facts are inconsistent, science should confess ignorance ('I am ignorant') rather than indulge in premature system-making. Progress may require generations of work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish unreal/self-contradictory facts from misclassified real facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Some alleged facts (e.g., astrology, witchcraft) are unreal and self-contradictory and cannot be reduced to law; other practices (e.g., alchemy) involve real facts misclassified and may become science when properly studied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When tempted to adopt non-scientific methods, first inquire whether the elements of the problem are superstition/unreal; if real, improved classification and method may turn the field into legitimate science.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophical method versus scientific method
rubrics_metrics.description: The philosophical method reaches judgments by internal cogitation rather than classification of facts and is thus dangerously liable to individual bias and to producing many competing contradictory systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophical methods cannot substitute for scientific method in producing universally valid knowledge or a real theory of morals; science's empirical, classificatory approach is preferred for truth and civic training.

rubrics_metrics.name: Touchstone of science: universal validity
rubrics_metrics.description: The touchstone of science is the universal validity of its results for all normally constituted and duly instructed minds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Metaphysical systems that fail to show universal validity are classified as imaginative rather than as solid contributions to knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disciplined imagination in discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: Creative imagination is the faculty by which a single statement or brief formula (a scientific law) is discovered to summarize a wide range of facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imagination is essential but must be disciplined: the proposed law must be tested and criticised exhaustively by its discoverer to ensure agreement with the whole group of phenomena (examples: Darwin, Faraday).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequence of scientific work: classify → hypothesize law → test
rubrics_metrics.description: An elaborate classification of facts and tracing their relationships is followed by the imaginative discovery of a concise law, which must then be tested and criticised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin's account is offered as illustration: collect facts by 'true Baconian principles' without theory, then develop a theory, subject it to long self-criticism and only later publish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding premature system-making
rubrics_metrics.description: It is idle to be impatient or to indulge in system-making where classification of facts is inadequate; cautious and laborious classification must come first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples (Galileo, the Atlantic cable) show that tasks once thought impossible required long periods of fact-gathering and reclassification before solutions emerged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Science as necessary training for citizenship
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific training — appreciation of evidence, classification of facts, and elimination of personal bias — is essential preparation for modern citizenship and the formation of moral/social judgments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A moral or social judgment that tends to social welfare depends first on knowledge and method rather than on self-sacrifice alone; citizens should form votes and judgments based on informed scientific method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific results influencing social policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific conclusions (e.g., theories of heredity such as Weismann's) can have direct bearing on moral conduct and duties of the state and society (education, Poor Law, charities).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even tentative scientific theories may profoundly affect policy; therefore one must heed scientific classification of facts and observations when making social decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of permanent 'Ignorabimus' claims
rubrics_metrics.description: To declare certain problems permanently unknowable ('Ignorabimus') is a dangerous modesty approaching despair; better to admit present ignorance and expect future progress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical precedent (cosmical problems solved after centuries) argues against asserting eternal limits to human knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justification for support of pure science
rubrics_metrics.description: Pure science is justified not only by its practical applications but also by its role in training imagination, aesthetic judgment, and providing foundations that often become the basis for future technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples (Galvani → telegraph, Hertz → applications of electromagnetic waves) show pure research often leads to major practical revolutions; this justifies state endowment and universal training in scientific methods.
